thread.title_full: United States has already lost World Cup with its greed and hostility | Opinion - NewsBreak

author: Nancy Armour
title: United States has already lost World Cup with its greed and hostility | Opinion - NewsBreak
text:
By Nancy Armour ,
5 hours ago President Donald Trump speaks as he receives the FIFA Peace Prize alongside FIFA President Gianni Infantino. By BRENDAN SMIALOWSKI, AFP via Getty Images IRVINE, CA ‒ The United States has already lost this World Cup .
The U.S. men’s national team could make a historically deep run and the tournament could be filled with wondrous goals and compelling games. It will not change the fact that we have shown ourselves to be a hateful and greedy nation, one where leaders are only willing to welcome a world as they want to see it rather than as it exists, and the love of the game is exploited for top dollar.
That will be the legacy, and the shame, of this World Cup. This is a once-in-a-generation opportunity to showcase the best of the United States and embrace the joy that soccer brings the rest of the world and, instead, we chose to be ugly Americans.
The World Cup is magical, unlike any sporting event we typically see in the United States. Crowds of Brazilians, all in that familiar canary-yellow jersey, chanting, singing and having a marvelous time. The Dutch turning the streets around the stadium into a sea of orange. Japanese fans cleaning up stadiums after games are over.
You cannot help but be won over by the spectacle, and anyone who experiences it comes away feeling the world is a little bit smaller and a whole lot friendlier than we might have thought.
“All these people, they want to enjoy a moment of happiness, a moment where their day-to-day problems can be left aside and they can just enjoy the game,” FIFA President Gianni Infantino said in his news conference Wednesday, June 10.
“Cry if their team loses or cry if their team wins, and just feel this emotion in community with others.”
That’s the tragedy of all this. Instead of letting the World Cup unite us, we’ve used it as an excuse to divide.
Iran, visas and ticket prices overshadow World Cup Infantino glossed over the hostility to Iran’s team , characterizing it as a triumph that they’re even participating when their treatment has been shameful. Iran had to move its base camp to Mexico at the eleventh hour, isn’t allowed to stay in the United States despite all three of its group games being here, and lost its allotment of tickets for fans.
He also downplayed the U.S. decision to deny entry to Somali referee Omar Artan . Artan, who has officiated World Cup qualifiers and the Under-20 World Cup last year, is one of several people turned away at the U.S. border for dubious reasons.
"We're working very closely to make sure the right people come into our country," President Donald Trump said Wednesday when asked about the rejections.
But the U.S. is supposed to be a World Cup host, not a World Cup bouncer.
World Cup should be party for all When you throw a global party, that means you have to welcome everyone, not just the folks you like. You don’t have to be happy Iran or a referee from Somalia is here. But you do have to show them the same courtesy as you do people from, say, Spain or Argentina.
We can’t even manage that.
"This is anathema to what this tournament is supposed to be about,” New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani said earlier this week when asked about the visa restrictions .
“If we can't even allow the players, the teams and journalists covering those teams to come to this country, it begs the larger question about our commitment to the spirit of this tournament,” Mamdani said. “We want this to be a tournament that reflects our commitment to us being part of something larger than ourselves.”
Ordinary fans priced out of World Cup That commitment to the spirit of the World Cup has been suspect since tickets were priced so high they’re almost impossible for ordinary fans to afford.
What makes soccer the beautiful game is that it’s accessible to anyone. Your race, your ethnicity, your gender, your religion, your socioeconomic status – none of it matters. So long as you have a ball and some space, you can play.
The World Cup ought to reflect that. But this tournament is shaping up to be no different than the Super Bowl or the Final Four, one more “experience” on the bucket list of the corporate set.
Hosting the World Cup could have been transformative for the United States. It could have drawn us closer to the rest of the world, and given us a new appreciation for people and places previously unfamiliar to us.
It also could have reminded the world of the United States’ power for good. We are, in general, a good-natured people, outgoing and approachable. Imagine the impression we could have made, the distrusts and disappointments we could have erased.
Instead, we chose to show the world our worst selves. It is the biggest loss of the World Cup.
Follow USA TODAY Sports columnist Nancy Armour on social media @nrarmour.
